newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Civil servants stage walkout in Montserrat.
newsitem.headline: Civil servants stage walkout in Montserrat.

text.p: Civil servants in Montserrat staged a walkout on Tuesday over pay and working conditions they say have deteriorated sharply since the island's volcano began erupting two years ago.
Officials said the protest had crippled many government agencies, affecting hospitals, customs services and public works as well as other departments.
"Most government departments have been affected," said Eugene Skerritt, permanent secretary to the chief minister.

It was not certain how many workers took part in the protest, which exacerbated already difficult conditions on the Caribbean island. New eruptions from the Soufriere Hills volcano have virtually destroyed the abandoned capital, Plymouth.

Emergency sirens wailed early on Tuesday in advance of a small eruption that sent ash and hot gases 8,000 (2,440 metres) feet into the air and forced residents to flee the island's central zone, officials said.

Skerritt said the civil service job action appeared to be in protest of pay and work conditions, and in support of overworked nurses who have laboured in stressful circumstances since the volcano came to life.
Nearly two dozen nurses have resigned in the last few months, some taking early retirement and others leaving the island entirely -- many citing the insecurity created by the volcano, officials said.
Compounding the stress, many civil servants have lost their homes to destructive flows of hot rock, ash and gases that have overrun the capital, Skerritt said.
"My feeling is the combination of all these different factors and the tremendous stress on them, in what is almost battle conditions, war conditions, is leading to this dissatisfaction," he said.
Montserrat government workers had not had a pay increase since 1990.

More than 1,000 people worked in government service before the volcano began spewing ash and rock in July 1995. It was uncertain how many remained, but most government departments were operating, "some in a more limited way," Skerritt said.
The government planned to give civil servants two months pay in addition to their regular salaries this month, and to hold workshops and counselling sessions in an effort to ease stress, he said.
Residents remaining on the island, fewer than half the pre-volcano population of 11,000, are crammed into homes and public shelters in the "safe zone" at the north end.
